newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-EA-Generali meet before CA deadline.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EA-Generali meet before CA deadline.

text.p: As a final Friday deadline for topped-up offers for Austrian selloff candidate Creditanstalt loomed, a diverse group led by insurer EA-Generali met on Wednesday to consider last-minute improvements to its offer.

A spokesman for the disillusioned consortium, outbid by rival Bank Austria by some three billion schillings ($275.2 million), said there would be no statement following the meeting at the Italian-controlled insurer's central Vienna headquarters.
"We're meeting to consider our next steps. I don't expect we will have a statement before Friday," he told Reuters.

EA-Generali's chances of getting control of Austria's second-largest bank have faded rapidly since market leader Bank Austria entered the seven-year race for the government's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt last month.

Bank Austria, controlled by the City of Vienna, is the preferred candidate of the ruling Social Democrats. Their junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, backs the consortium, but Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima insists he must sell to the best bidder.

EA-Generali and its partners, which include savings bank Die Erste EOSVp.VI, Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commercialie Italiana, have offered a total of 13.8 billion schillings for the state's 19.9 million shares in the bank and want to sell about a quarter of those on the market.
Bank Austria has bid some 16.8 billion schillings for the entire bank stake. No details of an outside offer by maverick entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek have been released.

The testy political atmosphere surrounding Europe's longest running privatisation was set to plunge to a new low this week with both parties holding separate meetings to map out their plans on how to end the country's privatisation quagmire.

The conservatives have called for a special session of parliament on January 14 to debate the sale and have warned Klima against making any definitive decision before that, threatening a collapse of the already creaky coalition.

But the Generali-led hotchpotch of international financial and industrial interests already last week signalled it would be hard pressed to come up with the extra money to match Bank Austria's bid, saying they had all but given up hope of getting their hands on the country's most traditional bank.

The conservatives on Tuesday made a last effort to appease their increasingly impatient coalition partner, saying they might agree to a sale of half the state's holding in Creditanstalt to Bank Austria if the other half was widely spread over the Vienna bourse.

In return, Klima signalled he may be willing to agree to take Bank Austria out of the fold of the City of Vienna. That prospect, however, has scared investors, who fear the bank may lose its AAA rating if it had to do without the municipality's credit backing.

Investors have reacted nervously to the increasingly murky debate over the sale of Austria's flagship bank. On Wednesday, both EA-Generali and Bank Austria were down some 2.5 percent in midday trade in an overall steady Vienna market.
